analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover emergency care, specialists, and clinical trials and gives patients independent appeals of denied claims.
analysis.headline: Despite 104 cosponsors, the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 2004 never received a House vote; it remained in committee and subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set national patient-protection standards for group health plans and insurers under three federal laws. It would require plans to run proper utilization-review programs, decide claims quickly, allow internal appeals, and submit certain denials to binding review by independent medical reviewers. It would also guarantee access to emergency care, specialists, obstetric and gynecological care, prescription drugs, and clinical trials, prohibit plans from financially rewarding decisions that deny claims, create a fund to help consumers navigate insurance disputes, and offer a tax credit to small businesses buying health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in employer group health plans and private health insurance, who would gain guaranteed access standards, faster claim decisions, and a binding external appeal when a plan denies care. Patients with serious or chronic conditions would benefit most, since the appeal rights apply to denials based on medical necessity. Doctors and other licensed providers would gain protections against plan interference and discrimination, and small businesses would be eligible for a new tax credit on health insurance expenses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients in employer and private health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans and insurers to decide initial claims quickly, decide expedited cases within 72 hours when a doctor certifies delay would jeopardize health, and give written, understandable reasons for any denial [S2] [S3].

Gives patients the right to internal appeals of denials with at least 180 days to file, and to an independent external review whose decisions are binding on the plan, with daily and per-case penalties for officials who refuse to authorize coverage an external reviewer approved [S3].
Bars utilization-review compensation arrangements that encourage denial of claims, and prohibits interference with doctor-patient communications [S2] [S3].

Guarantees access to emergency care, timely specialist care, obstetric and gynecological care, pediatric care, prescription drugs, clinical trials, and minimum hospital stays after mastectomy [S2] [S3].
Creates a Health Care Consumer Assistance Fund of grants to states to run toll-free hotlines and consumer help offices for people fighting coverage problems [S3].
Provides a tax credit for small businesses' health insurance expenses and grants to help small employers obtain coverage information [S2] [S3].
Opens civil remedies under ERISA (the law governing most employer health plans), which since the 1980s has sharply limited patients' ability to sue over denied care from employer plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the cost of compliance: running qualified utilization-review and appeals programs, paying for independent external reviews, covering mandated services like clinical trials and longer mastectomy stays, and paying penalties when they ignore external review decisions. Some of those compliance and coverage costs would likely be passed on through premiums and benefits, and insurers would lose a tool they had used to limit payouts under ERISA's narrow legal remedies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers sponsoring health plans

drawbacks.text: The compliance and coverage mandates would raise administrative and benefit costs for insurers and for employers funding group plans, and those costs would likely flow partly into higher premiums or leaner benefits for workers [S2] [S3].

The external review process cannot force a plan to cover services that are specifically excluded or limited in plain-language plan documents, so the appeal rights apply to medical judgments rather than to the scope of coverage a plan has written for itself [S3].
Patients seeking external review could be charged a filing fee of up to $25 unless they are indigent or the plan waives internal review, a modest but real barrier for some claimants [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people covered by employer and private plans, the appeal rights, timeliness rules, and access guarantees addressed a real and widely experienced problem: plan denials with no practical way to fight back under ERISA. The main cost is higher premiums and administrative burden on insurers and employers, and the bill's own design limits appeals to medical judgments while leaving explicit coverage exclusions untouched. On balance the protections for patients are substantial and the drawbacks are the ordinary cost of regulation, but the bill never got far enough for those trade-offs to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2004 and referred to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, and it never received a markup, floor vote, or any further action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 2004 on June 21, 2004, with more than 50 original cosponsors listed on the bill [S1] [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
On July 19, 2004, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and on September 7, 2004, to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations; no further action followed [S5].
The bill accumulated 104 cosponsors, 103 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The bill never came to a vote in either chamber, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group health plans are better off, because they avoided federal patient-protection standards, binding external review of claim denials, and civil liability under ERISA. Patients who needed a way to contest denied care did not get one in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 103 of the 104 cosponsors were Democrats, with just one Republican, and the bill received no consideration in the Republican-controlled House committees or floor.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would impose utilization-review standards, fast claim timelines, binding independent external appeals, coverage mandates, and financial penalties on plans that ignore reviewer decisions. Insurers profit by controlling what care is paid for, so their interest in defeating these standards ran directly against patients' interest in contesting denials.

Under ERISA, employer plans faced new federal standards and, through the civil remedies title, greater exposure to lawsuits over denied care, with compliance costs likely passed to workers through premiums.

industries.industry: Physicians and other licensed health care providers
industries.note: The bill bars plans from interfering with doctor-patient communications, from discriminating against providers by licensure, and from incentive arrangements that reward denial decisions, and it protects patient advocacy.

industries.industry: Independent external review entities and medical reviewers
industries.note: The bill creates a certified, paid role for outside review organizations deciding disputes over claim denials, with plans required to bear the costs of the review process.
A tax credit for small-business health insurance expenses and grants for coverage information would lower the cost of providing coverage to small employers.
